Chapter 18, Mokṣasaṃnyāsayoga, the Yoga of Liberation and Renunciation, is the Gītā's longest chapter and its summation. Arjuna opens by asking Kṛṣṇa to distinguish saṃnyāsa, the renunciation of action itself, from tyāga, the renunciation of its fruit — and Kṛṣṇa answers that action cannot simply be abandoned, since even the body's maintenance is action; what can and must be given up is attachment to the results. He sorts this renunciation, like everything else in the chapter, into the three guṇas: tyāga done from delusion, from aversion to what is merely difficult, or truly, from duty performed without clinging to its fruit. The same threefold analysis is then run across the five factors that make up any action (the seat of action, the agent, the instruments, the many kinds of effort, and fate), and across knowledge, action, the agent, intellect, steadfastness, and happiness in turn — each shown in its sattva-, rajas-, and tamas-natured forms, from clear-sighted knowledge that sees the one in the many down to the deluded stubbornness or joyless pleasure that mistakes darkness for peace. The chapter then grounds this in the divisions of society: the duties of brahmin, kṣatriya, vaiśya, and śūdra are shown to arise from each person's own nature, and devotion to one's own duty, however imperfect, is declared better than another's performed well — because every action, offered up without attachment, becomes a means to liberation through disciplined intellect and self-mastery, culminating in Kṛṣṇa's supreme instruction to abandon all duties and come to him alone for refuge. The chapter, and the poem, close with instructions on how this teaching is to be transmitted and honored, Arjuna's declaration that his delusion is dispelled and he will act on Kṛṣṇa's word, and Sañjaya's own closing testimony to the wonder of what he has been privileged to hear.
